title: Ethiopian Spiced Chicken Stew
community: All of Ethiopia — the most important dish in the national cuisine
author: Mama Tigist

heritage.origin: All of Ethiopia — the dish that defines the nation's food identity
heritage.history: Doro Wat is Ethiopia's national dish — the deeply red, intensely spiced chicken stew with whole hard-boiled eggs that is served at every celebration. Christmas (Genna), Easter (Fasika), weddings, name days, and the Ethiopian New Year (Enkutatash) all begin and end with Doro Wat. The preparation is sacred: the chicken must be cut into exactly 12 pieces (representing the 12 apostles in Orthodox tradition), the eggs must be boiled whole and pierced before adding to absorb the berbere, and the cooking must be done with patience and ceremony. Doro Wat is also the centrepiece of the Ethiopian mesob — the large communal injera platter from which a family eats together. It is simultaneously the most time-consuming and most important dish in the cuisine.

desc: Ethiopian Doro Wat — the national dish of Ethiopia. A whole chicken cut into 12 pieces, marinated in lemon and salt, then slow-simmered for 2.5 hours in a deeply red berbere sauce built on dry-caramelised onions and kibbeh, with whole boiled eggs pierced to absorb the sauce. The dish that defines Ethiopian cuisine.
longDesc: Doro Wat cannot be rushed — the 2.5 hours of slow simmering is not excessive but necessary. The chicken must be marinated first in lemon and salt to remove the raw smell (this is called 'washing the chicken' in the Ethiopian tradition). The onions must be dry-caramelised without oil for 30 minutes. The berbere must toast in the kibbeh. The chicken must simmer until the sauce coats the back of a spoon and every piece of chicken is falling-tender. The eggs must be pierced and added in the final 20 minutes to turn deep orange-red. There are no shortcuts in Doro Wat.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken (1.5 kg) — cut into 12 pieces
6 hard-boiled eggs — pierced all over with a fork
equipment: Large heavy clay pot or Dutch oven
steps: Marinate the chicken: toss the 12 pieces with lemon juice and salt. Rest 30 minutes. Rinse and pat dry.

Dry caramelise the onions: place diced onions in the dry clay pot — NO OIL, NO WATER. Cook over medium heat, stirring often, for 25—30 minutes until very dark golden and caramelised. This is the most important step.
Add kibbeh to the caramelised onions. Stir to melt and combine. Cook 3 minutes.
Add berbere. Stir continuously into the kibbeh-onion base. Toast for 4—5 minutes — the berbere must cook in the fat.
Add garlic, ginger, and tomato paste. Stir for 2—3 minutes.
Add chicken pieces. Stir to coat every piece in the berbere sauce.
Add stock or water. Bring to a boil.
Reduce to lowest heat. Cover and simmer 90—100 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Pierce the hard-boiled eggs all over with a fork — very deeply so the sauce can penetrate.
Add pierced eggs to the sauce. Continue simmering covered for 20 more minutes.
The sauce should be very thick, deeply red, and coating the chicken and eggs.
Season. The Doro Wat is ready when the sauce coats the back of a spoon and the chicken is falling-tender.
chefTips: 30 minutes of dry-caramelised onions — the absolute foundation. No shortcuts. No oil.
6 tablespoons of berbere seems excessive until you eat it — this quantity is correct.
The chicken must be marinated in lemon and salt for at least 30 minutes — this is the Ethiopian technique for 'cleaning' the raw chicken smell.
Pierce the eggs very deeply — a fork does not penetrate far enough. Use a skewer. The eggs should turn deep orange-red throughout.
Doro Wat made the day before is dramatically better — the flavours develop overnight.
The finished sauce should be so thick that it barely pours.
commonMistakes: Adding oil with onions — dry-caramelise only.
Not piercing the eggs deeply enough.
Short cooking time — the sauce must be very thick.
cookingScience: Doro Wat cooking involves three sequential chemical transformations: (1) The dry Maillard caramelisation of onion sugars over 30 minutes concentrates their glutamates and sweetness without the dilution effect of fat. (2) The berbere's fat-soluble carotenoids (responsible for the red colour) dissolve into the kibbeh — this can only happen in fat. (3) The chicken's collagen converts to gelatin over 90+ minutes of gentle simmering, naturally thickening the sauce. The pierced eggs absorb the berbere through osmotic pressure as they cool in the sauce.
sustainabilityTips: Whole chicken used completely — the 12 cuts include every part. Ethiopian cooking never wastes.
servedWith: On the full mesob celebration platter
storage: Refrigerate 5 days. Freeze 3 months. Dramatically improves overnight.
reheating: Gently on stovetop — add a splash of water if needed.
healthBenefits: Berbere contains powerful antioxidants and anti-inflammatory compounds.
Kibbeh provides fat-soluble vitamins A and D.
Garlic and ginger are antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory.
The eggs provide complete protein and additional B vitamins.
culturalNote: Doro Wat is Ethiopia — not as an approximation but as an exact truth. Every Ethiopian celebration begins with the aroma of onions dry-caramelising on the fire. Every Ethiopian who has lived abroad says the same thing: the first meal they cook when they feel homesick is Doro Wat. The dish has been the centrepiece of Ethiopian hospitality for as long as anyone can remember. To be offered Doro Wat by an Ethiopian family is to be offered the most important thing in their kitchen.
